memory_candidates.content: Under `set -euo pipefail`, a bare assignment `var=$(cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3)` is NOT exempt from `set -e`: if the first command in the pipe exits non-zero (e.g. `grep` finding no match) while later commands (`tail`, `cut`) exit 0, `pipefail` still propagates the failure through the whole pipeline's exit status, and the plain assignment form silently aborts the script right there -- before any subsequent `if [ -n "$var" ]` branch or later diagnostic output ever runs. This is easy to miss because the failure produces no error message at all. Fix: append `|| true` to the assignment whenever an empty/no-match result from the pipeline is a valid, expected outcome that the following code already branches on.

When an agent/skill instruction file embeds a concrete, ready-to-copy Markdown/code skeleton for an artifact, that inline skeleton wins over a separately-documented format spec even when the spec is force-injected into every dispatch prompt and a real-time hook also checks compliance after every write. Advisory cross-references and even in-band hooks lose to a concrete, later, copy-pasteable instruction in the same file the agent is actively following. When a generated artifact diverges from its own format spec across many historical instances, look first for a competing inline template in the generating agent's own instructions, and fix that template in place rather than adding a third cross-reference or check.

A whole-document `grep -qF "**Field**:"` style metadata-presence check can pass on prose that merely quotes the field name in running text (e.g. a Verification section describing 'the old `**Completed**:` header'), even when the real metadata block has been deleted. This is a real edge case for validators that check field presence by simple substring match rather than by scoping to a metadata block; a negative-control test on such a validator can produce a smaller-than-expected missing-field list for this reason, which is a validator characteristic to note honestly rather than a test failure.
